name: Freyr's Sword
aliases: The Sword That Fights by Itself
powers: Fights of its own accord, without a hand to wield it.
description: Freyr's sword is the magic blade of the god Freyr that fights by itself, without a hand to wield it. In Skírnismál, Freyr gives the sword to his servant Skírnir as payment for wooing the giantess Gerðr on his behalf — a gift of the self-fighting sword in exchange for love. The loss is fatal at Ragnarök: the Prose Edda recounts that Freyr, lacking his good sword, fights the fire giant Surtr and falls, having given away his only weapon. The sword is thus remembered in the Eddas as the price of love and the cause of a god's death, and it is often read as a parable of how love and war can demand the same sacrifice. It remains a standard example in discussions of the self-acting weapons of myth, and the tale of the sword given away for Gerðr is retold in most modern versions of the Eddas.

name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
powers: Lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon.
description: Freyja's falcon cloak, also called the feather cloak or fjaðrhamr, is a garment of feathers that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. In the Prose Edda the cloak is kept by the goddess Freyja and lent out when the gods need swift flight: Loki borrows it to search for the goddess Iðunn after the giant Þjazi carries her off, and later uses it to pursue Þjazi, who had taken the shape of an eagle, back to the walls of Asgard where the gods kill him. In the poem Þrymskviða, Freyja's cloak is likewise the means by which Loki flies out to steal back the hammer Mjölnir. Shape-shifting feather-cloaks appear elsewhere in Norse legend, most famously in the story of the smith Völund and his swan-maiden bride. Freyja's falcon cloak is the standard example of the feathered flying garment of Norse myth.

name: Swedish Folk Costume
material: Wool and linen with silver and embroidery
description: The Swedish folk costume (folkdräkt), the regional dress of parish and province, worn for work and festivals and gradually codified from the 18th century. Each district had its own colours, cut, embroidery, and accessories such as the flounced apron and the bodice. The national costume, the Sverigedräkt, was created in 1903 by Märta Jörgensen and has since been widely adopted. In the countryside the dress told every beholder where a person came from: the cut of the skirt, the shape of the bodice, and the colour of the stockings changed from parish to parish, and the right to wear certain garments was guarded with pride. Wool and linen were woven and dyed at home, while the silver buckles and brooches that fastened the clothes were the work of the village smith. When the folk costume died out in the later nineteenth century it was preserved by the museums, and in the twentieth it was revived for national holidays — most famously the blue-and-yellow Sverigedräkt, which remains Sweden's most worn ceremonial dress.

name: The Flower of Happiness
maker: Grows at Sunnymount Crest in the tale
powers: Possessing it was said to bring happiness.
description: The flower of happiness, the marvel of a tale told at Sunnymount Crest: a flower whose possession, or whose bloom, was said to bring happiness to whoever found it. In the tale the search for the flower tests the seeker, and the happiness it brings is measured in the finding rather than in any magic of the blossom itself. The tale belongs to the great European family of quests for a thing of pure good fortune, from the golden apple to the singing tree, where the journey works the change in the hero. At Sunnymount Crest the flower is tied to a real place, and the story shapes how the landscape is remembered. The flower is an object-lesson of the wonder-tale rather than a real plant, a reminder that happiness is found by those who seek it well.

name: The Flying Trunk
powers: Carries its owner through the air to wherever he wishes.
description: The enchanted wooden trunk of Andersen's tale, given to a spendthrift merchant's son by his father and used by its owner to fly through the air to the land of the Turks and court a princess in her tower. When he squanders his remaining coins on fireworks to amuse the court, a spark sets the trunk alight, and it burns to ash, leaving him wandering the world with a story no one believes. The tale plays the magic object as both luck and ruin, and the trunk itself is one of Andersen's most famous flying vehicles, built on older folk motifs of the magical vehicle.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Den flyvende kuffert (1839)

name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
powers: Doomed to sail the Cape of Good Hope forever; sighting it is an omen.
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman is a spectral East Indiaman of Dutch maritime legend, doomed to sail the waters off the Cape of Good Hope for ever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, Falkenberg or the Vanderdecken, swore a blasphemous oath in the teeth of a storm. Mariners reported seeing the phantom vessel from the seventeenth century onward, often glowing with a supernatural light, and a sighting was taken as a warning of disaster or death at sea. The legend was spread by travellers' and sailors' tales in the 1830s, and Richard Wagner's opera Der fliegende Holländer of 1843 fixed the story of the captain condemned to sail until redeemed by a woman's love. No physical vessel survives or ever existed, and the tale is classed as maritime folklore rather than history. The ship has been retold in poems, novels and films, making the Flying Dutchman the archetype of the haunted ship.
source: Maritime legend, from the seventeenth century

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
powers: Shaken by Frau Holle, its feathers fall to earth as snow.
description: Frau Holle's feather bed is the great bedding that the old woman shakes out in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Frau Holle' (KHM 24), causing its feathers to fall to earth as snow. The industrious heroine, after her fall into the well and a period of service shaking the bed each morning, is rewarded with a shower of gold, while the lazy sister earns only pitch. The tale explains the seasons through household labour, the winter snow being nothing more than Frau Holle's feathers flying. Frau Holle herself, a fair, long-toothed old woman who rewards diligence and punishes idleness, is sometimes identified by scholars with the Germanic goddess Holda of folklore, who was said to shake her feather pillows to make snow. The episode is among the most famous comic explanations in the Grimms' collection. The feather bed is the story's hinge, turning domestic work into the natural world's weather.

name: Franks Casket
description: The Franks Casket, also called the Auzon Casket, is an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, about 23 centimetres long, with panels bearing scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, framed by inscriptions in runes and Latin. Its front panel shows the smith Weland being released by the maiden Beadohild after his imprisonment by King Nithhad, while the right panel shows the Adoration of the Magi, a pairing of pagan and Christian imagery typical of the period. The runic inscriptions, including a cryptic challenge in Old English verse, make the casket one of the most studied objects in early English archaeology. It was bought in the nineteenth century by the antiquarian Augustus Franks after being found at Auzon in France, and is now in the British Museum, with one panel in the Bargello in Florence. The casket's mixture of whalebone, runes and interwoven legends marks it as a key witness to Anglo-Saxon storytelling.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
powers: The counterweight of truth against which the heart of the dead is weighed.
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, goddess of truth, order, and justice, and placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth. Ma'at herself is rarely shown without it, and the hieroglyph for the feather stands for her name and for the idea of justice itself. In later and modern thought it has become a byword for fair judgment, and the phrase 'feather of truth' is now used far beyond Egyptology.

name: Flaming Pearl
description: The flaming pearl, huozhu, is a luminous orb wreathed in curling flame that Chinese art shows two dragons chasing or guarding, and it is one of the most common motifs of East Asian decoration. The image appears on temple roofs, ceramic dishes, paintings, and lanterns, and its meaning draws on several layers: in Buddhist iconography the pearl is the cintamani, the wish-granting jewel that fulfils every desire, while in Daoist cosmology it can stand for the moon, the sun, or the inner pearl of spiritual refinement. The dragon that guards the pearl is usually the celestial dragon of rain and water, and the chase motif is sometimes read as the play of yin and yang or of the sun and moon across the heavens. In folk belief the pearl is also linked to the treasure of the dragon's undersea palace, and stories tell of heroes who descend to the sea king's court for the jewel. Whatever the reading, the flaming pearl carries a consistent charge of wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it remains the standard companion of the dragon in pan-Asian art.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The four white umbrellas are the tiered white standards that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings of the Bagan and later dynasties, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. In the creation tale of kingship, the story of Thagya Min and the first king, the white umbrella is the mark of the king chosen by heaven, and the number of umbrellas carried over a ruler marked his rank, with the great white umbrella of the king symbolizing the highest authority. The image of the king as the bearer of the white umbrella survives in the Hmannan Yazawin chronicle and in the coronation imagery of the Burmese court, and the umbrella standard still crowns Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority. The same iconography is shared with Thailand and Laos, where the tiered white parasol is the emblem of the Buddhist king. The four umbrellas bind earthly sovereignty to the blessing of the nats, the spirits who watch over the realm.

name: False Face Mask
material: Carved basswood with red and black paint
powers: Wards off sickness with the power of the forest spirits.
description: The False Face masks of the Haudenosaunee are distorted human faces carved from living basswood, painted red and black, and used by the False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness from the sick. The twisted features recall the forest beings of tradition, above all the Great Face who is said to have broken his own face in a contest with the sun and gained power over disease, appearing in the story of the Flying Head. Traditionally the masks are carved from the living tree without metal tools, so the bark and spirit of the tree remain part of the carving, and they are kept by society members where tobacco can be offered to them. Historically the masks were never sold; their acquisition by museums and collectors in the late twentieth century became a major controversy, and some collections have since returned them. Worn by dancers who blow warm ashes over the patient, the masks embody the being that both causes and cures sickness.

name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
description: The asen is the commemorative altar staff of the Fon of Benin, a forged iron pole topped with a figurative scene, an ancestor at work, an animal, a scene of daily life, set in a base of clay or iron and placed beside the ancestor altar of the compound. When a family member dies, an asen is raised for the dead, and through it the ancestor receives offerings during the rites of remembrance and is fed and spoken with as if still present. The iron is worked by smiths, who are themselves set apart in Fon society, and the figures are made to be read: a hunter with his gun, a woman at the mortar, the emblems of the life the dead one lived. The asen is central to the Vodun practice of ancestor veneration, and older pieces, their iron darkened with age and offerings, are valued in museums as records of Dahomey's families. In the compound, the row of asen is the visible genealogy of the household.
source: Fon ancestor ritual; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Fijian Masi (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Fiji, beaten by women from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into broad sheets, which are felted together on a wooden anvil and painted with geometric designs in black, brown and red. Masi is made in working parties for gifts, dress and ceremony: it wraps the body at weddings and funerals, lines the walls of the chiefly house, and the finest decorated pieces are given on occasions of state. The patterns are handed down within clans, whose history the cloth records, and the same barkcloth family is known across the Pacific — masi in Fiji, siapo in Samoa, ngatu in Tonga, kapa in Hawai'i — with each island giving the craft its own style.
source: Ethnographic records of Fijian material culture

name: Fijian War Club
description: Carved club of the Fijian islands, made from the dense wood of the vesi (ironwood) or Pacific casuarina and shaped in a wide range of named forms: the long-bladed ulato, the throwing club, the bulbous totokia with its blunt striking head, and ceremonial clubs inlaid with shell or whalebone. War clubs were the emblem of the Fijian warrior and badges of rank, carried by chiefs as symbols of office and passed down as named trophies and treasures whose owners' histories were remembered. Some were also laid with chiefs in burial, and clubs and whale teeth together formed the ceremonial wealth used to seal alliances and settle the fiercest disputes.

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a very long overtone flute of the Slovak shepherds, the central instrument of the Podpoľanie region, made from elder, maple or ash wood and reaching 160 to 200 centimetres in length, with a short side tube that carries the wind to the main bore. It has only three finger holes, yet a skilled player produces a low, humming bass and high, crying overtones by overblowing, and the traditional repertoire imitates the gurgle of springs, the wind and long pastoral calls. Shepherds played the fujara while tending flocks on the slopes of Poľana, and each maker decorated the instrument individually with burnt or carved ornament, so no two fujaras are alike. UNESCO proclaimed the fujara and its music a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008, and it is now heard both at folk festivals in Detva and in concert music.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art. The feather is usually the first test: the hero who takes it must then capture the living bird, often with a golden cage, and afterwards the horse with the golden mane and the fair princess Vasilisa. Because the bird is otherworldly, its feather is sometimes said to burn whatever it touches and to heal the sick if kept near. The motif later inspired Stravinsky's 1910 ballet 'The Firebird', which made the glowing feather a worldwide image of Russian fairy-tale art.
